title: Written Statement of David Owens, member of the Board of Directors of ESPX Global Inc., for Panel 1 The State of Reliability in a Changing Energy Landscape Operational Challenges etc. for FERC's 10/21/2026 Reliability Technical Conference under AD26-8.

Lodie White
Office of Electric Reliability
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street, NE
Washington, DC 20426

Re: Reliability Technical Conference, Docket No. AD26-8-000 (October 21, 2026): Written Statement of David Owens, Panel 1

Dear Ms. White:

I appreciate the Commission's invitation to participate in the October 21, 2026 Reliability Technical Conference, Panel 1, “The State of Reliability in a Changing Energy Landscape – Operational Challenges of Integrating Large Loads in Evolving System Dynamics.”

I am a member of the Board of Directors of ESPX Global Inc., which develops software and analytics for battery energy storage, including methods for assessing storage availability and operating capability. My bio is attached. It reflects extensive experience in electric power grid reliability and regulation.

The Measurement of State of Charge in Real-Time Operations is Extremely Important
 
As battery storage becomes an increasingly important source of capacity, frequency response, voltage support, and other grid services, system operators need to know not only how much BESS capacity is installed, but how much capability is actually available at a given time and for how long. State of charge is a fundamental part of that determination. 

State of Charge Fills an Information Gap Threatening System Reliability 

As NERC has raised the threat of BESS uncertainty in recent NERC Long Term Reliability Assessments, the integration of Large Loads bringing large amounts of co-located BESS as back-up energy will further increase the information gap in both operational and planning studies of when and how much BESS capability is actually available to the grid.  The reliability framework should therefore place greater emphasis on measuring, validating and communicating the real-time availability of BESS capability.

Without new tools and reliability analysis that will accurately track today’s and tomorrow’s BESS performance, this uncertain information and measurement gap will grow much larger triggering greater deviations between expected versus actual deliverable power (MW) for a stated duration. 

BESS has so far been managed with operational rules that are intended to provide assurance to operators that energy is available when needed including the BESS SOC.  But today’s SOC telemetry reports a day-ahead estimate produced by the battery-management system of individual BESS owner, not a real-time direct measurement of stored energy by system operator or ISO.  What is needed is operational intelligence about BESS assets to assess actual BESS operating capability and availability. A critical piece to collecting this operational intelligence data is a common data set and format which can then be leveraged to close the gap between load growth and BESS SOC uncertainty for grid planners and operators.  

Better SOC Information Can Unlock Existing Storage Capability and Lower Investment Costs and Tariff

Today’s diverse practices and tariffs that seek to minimize the risk of BESS shortfalls will leave increasing amounts of valuable MW out of operational and planning time horizon studies. These practices are also imposing investment in BESS assets above rated net output to ensure sufficient headroom to meet schedules. PJM is solicitating new ideas and modeling solutions to overcome these major operational challenges.  I co-authored two Public Utilities Fortnightly articles illustrating this threat and provide a new solution.

In an April Public Utilities Fortnightly article, “Utility Scale Energy Storage – Underutilized and Overlooked,” it describes how existing rules and methodologies can prevent system planners and market operators from fully utilizing the capacity and energy available from energy storage resources (ESR). As a result, existing ESR capacity may remain underutilized even as new capacity is sought to meet planning reserve margins. To be consistent with the FERC Docket language, the terms ESR and BESS are used interchangeably onward.

The Commission posed six questions for Panel 1. The six questions examine whether existing planning and operating frameworks are adequate for a grid with rapidly growing large loads, increasing reliance on inverter-based resources, and new sources of operational and infrastructure risk. I therefore will focus on two questions, Number 2 and Number 3, as BESS is an important part of the solutions to these issues.

2) ERCOT is proposing to require advanced grid support functions (e.g., fast-frequency response and synthetic inertia) for future BESS in response to reliability events and operational trends such as frequency excursions, voltage instability, and IBR-driven oscillations.  Are these same issues present elsewhere, and should similar requirements be applied nationwide?
3) How should operators quantify and manage the reliability implications of declining system inertia in regions with rapid interconnection of large loads and where IBR penetration is accelerating and replacing conventional generation?
Firstly, Question 2: The issues ERCOT is responding to are not unique to ERCOT. The inverter-based resource performance problems that led to the Commission’s Order No. 901 were documented by NERC in both the Western and Texas Interconnections. ERCOT’s specific requirement should not be copied nationwide in identical form. The Commission should instead set common, performance-based principles that each region implements according to its own conditions. One element of those principles deserves particular attention. ERCOT’s requirement ensures that certain new BESS have specified advanced grid-support capability, but ERCOT has stated that it does not require the resource to reserve capacity or state of charge (SOC) to provide that support. Whether the support is actually available when a disturbance occurs therefore depends on information that system operators do not consistently receive or use today.  So what should the Commission consider to address this? I ask the Commission to consider a series of subordinate questions to Question 2 in order to fully grasp the risks of not incorporating accurate and predictable SOC for the forthcoming surge of BESS.

I provide commentary of why the Commission needs to consider these subordinate questions.  A comprehensive set of responses are provided as Appendix A to this testimony.
 
How many MW can a BESS resource reliably provide when needed, for how long, and with what degree of assurance?

Installed or nameplate MW should not be treated as a complete measure of a battery energy storage resource’s reliability contribution. A BESS resource may have a stated interconnection or inverter rating, but its ability to support the bulk power system at a particular time depends on whether it has sufficient stored energy, whether that energy is available for grid use, and whether the resource can sustain the required output for the relevant reliability interval.

2b, What determines whether a BESS can provide the required grid-support response, sustain it for the required duration, and recover its capability afterward?

Several different capabilities must be distinguished. The inverter and its controls determine whether the BESS can provide the required response characteristics, such as frequency or voltage response. The resource’s operating condition—including its available energy (MWh) and State of Charge (an estimate of charge level referenced to defined limits, which may be reported as a percentage)—helps determine whether that response can be sustained and how the resource can recover afterward.

2c. What role does State of Charge play in determining a BESS’s available and sustained operating capability?

State of Charge is a fundamental input to determining how much energy a BESS has available and therefore how long a given MW output can be sustained. Installed MW alone does not establish sustained capability because a battery with the same nameplate rating can have materially different operating capability depending on its energy state and recent operating history.

2d. What information is needed by system operators to determine BESS capability accurately and reliably in planning and real-time operations?

System operators need information that translates a BESS resource’s operating condition into usable system capability. Resource planning requires estimates of the dependable capability that BESS can provide under future system conditions

2e. How should such information be measured, validated, expressed consistently, and communicated to system operators?	

BESS capability should be determined from operating data that describe the resource’s power capability, usable stored energy, State of Charge, operating limits, and other constraints relevant to the service being evaluated. Where capability is projected rather than directly observed, the estimate should identify the applicable time horizon and the assumptions used to derive it.

2f. How should BESS operating-capability information be incorporated into resource-adequacy, unit-commitment, dispatch, and ancillary-service models?
	
Capability information has limited reliability value unless the models used for planning and operations can incorporate it. Resource-adequacy models should use appropriate measures of dependable BESS capability. 

2g.  Are the reliability events and operational trends prompting ERCOT’s BESS requirements also present in other regions?

Yes, in varying degrees. The severity of these issues varies with IBR penetration, system strength, and available inertia, so the Commission, NERC, and the ISOs/RTOs should determine where comparable reliability concerns exist and what performance requirements are warranted under regional system conditions.

2h. Should requirements similar to ERCOT’s advanced grid-support requirements for BESS be applied nationwide?

Not in identical form. Different regions have different resource mixes, network characteristics, operating conditions, and reliability needs. ERCOT in particular is connected to neighboring systems only through asynchronous ties, so it does not directly share their synchronous inertia; its requirement reflects that circumstance.

An appropriate national objective is to establish common principles where a common reliability need exists, and to allow region-specific performance parameters consistent with applicable national Reliability Standards, , rather than prescribe a particular control design or impose an identical implementation in every region.

2  Should the Commission establish common, performance-based reliability principles for BESS while allowing ISOs and RTOs to implement them according to regional system conditions?

Yes. The Commission should establish common reliability principles for BESS while allowing regional implementation. Those principles should focus on measurable performance, accurate and usable information about actual capability, and incorporation of that information into reliability planning and system operations.


Secondly, Question 3:  BESS can provide fast frequency response and, with suitable controls, synthetic inertial response, subject to available energy, power capability, and operating limits.  NERC reports that BESS in the Texas and Western Interconnections are contributing to improved frequency control and response.  Such support can reduce the operational impact of lower synchronous inertia. From what we understand, in the CAISO Market, BESS with primary frequency response act within a fraction of a second, injecting power to arrest a frequency decline far faster than conventional governors. In practice, this fast response has raised frequency nadirs and shortened the time to arrest following large generation losses, which reduces the operational impact of lower inertia.  However, NERC Reliability Standard BAL-003 can reflect sustained BESS contributions to aggregate frequency response, but its measurement method does not separately quantify initial response speed or all benefits to the frequency nadir. The Commission and NERC should examine whether complementary performance and energy-availability requirements are warranted. Adequate real-time SOC visibility should support assessment of whether such frequency support will be available when needed. 

Looking Ahead 

SOC accuracy is a viable piece of the puzzle for addressing resource adequacy, grid reliability services and affordability challenges. FERC Order No. 841 resulted in a patchwork of rules and practices that were approved in individual tariffs to implement BESS participation in capacity, energy, and ancillary services markets. There were technical challenges to how providers could obtain verifiable SOC.  By collecting BESS data that can be universally applied to analysis and new technology leveraging that data, changes to these tariffs can reflect new usable information for BESS SoC bringing both reliability and market benefits, The capability to fully integrate BESS into the grid at an equal footing as other resources are able to requires only the will to collaborate between FERC and, NERC, and investors, like utilities, and from operators/planners like ISO/RTOs. 

As more data centers are added, each with their own back up energy resources and each managing their load and resource planning with AI-dominant technology applied behind-the-meter, this uncertainty for BESS SOC will only grow larger and faster triggering greater deviations between expected available BESS resources and actual operable energy in real-time.  

In summary, the Commission should establish common national principles for BESS grid support, with implementation suited to regional conditions. The industry should also move toward a framework in which BESS capability—not simply BESS nameplate capacity—is visible, measurable, validated, and usable for reliability planning and real-time operations. Doing so would improve BESS’s benefits for reliability while also allowing the electric system to make better use of storage resources that have already been built.

Thank you for your consideration of this written statement.

Sincerely,

David Owens
Member, Board of Directors
ESPX Global Inc. 
1350 Beverly Road
Suite 115, PMB 293
McLean, VA 22101-3633

APPENDIX A 
Subordinate Questions to Panel 1 – Question 2

TESTIMONY OF DAVID K. OWENS
FERC RELIABILITY TECHNICAL CONFERENCE
October 21, 2026

How many MW can a BESS resource reliably provide when needed, for how long, and with what degree of assurance?

Installed or nameplate MW should not be treated as a complete measure of the reliability contribution of a battery energy storage system (BESS). A BESS resource may have a stated interconnection or inverter rating, but its ability to support the bulk power system at a particular time depends on whether it has sufficient stored energy, whether that energy is available for grid use, and whether the resource can sustain the required output for the required duration.
For reliability, planning, and market-accreditation purposes, system operators and regulators should distinguish among installed capacity, available capability, and sustained capability.
Installed capacity refers to the resource’s nominal MW rating. It is a static project characteristic and does not establish that the resource can provide that MW level during system-risk intervals, the periods when the system is most likely to need the resource.
Available capability refers to the MW the resource can provide at a particular time, after accounting for state of charge (SOC), available stored energy, equipment status, operating limits, derates, outage conditions, and any reserved-energy obligations. The accuracy of an estimate of available capability also depends on the quality of the underlying operating data.
Sustained capability refers to the MW level the resource can maintain for a specified duration. A battery that can inject 100 MW for 15 minutes is not equivalent, for reliability-accreditation purposes, to a resource that can inject 100 MW for four hours during a system stress event. The same principle applies to the active-power component of advanced grid-support functions, even though the relevant duration may be seconds or minutes rather than hours. The inverter may be technically capable of responding, while the resource may lack the headroom or stored energy needed to provide the response when the disturbance occurs, or may be prevented from providing it by operating limits or other conditions.
The relevant question is not the resource’s nameplate MW rating, but the MW-duration response it can provide for the reliability function at issue, under expected operating conditions, and with the level of assurance required by the applicable reliability standard, market rule, or accreditation method.
Accordingly, BESS reliability assessment should be expressed as a MW-duration capability profile in addition to its nameplate MW rating. The assessment should determine how much response the resource can provide, for how long, and with what demonstrated or modeled level of assurance. For resource adequacy, that may require assessing how many MW the resource can sustain for one hour, two hours, four hours, or other planning-relevant durations during system-risk intervals. For advanced grid-support functions, it may require assessing how much upward or downward response the resource can provide over sub-cycle, second, or minute timeframes, given its SOC, available energy, headroom, operating limits, and recent operating history. Voltage support should also be assessed in terms of reactive-power capability, inverter current limits, and control performance.
This assessment should be based on validated telemetry, SOC, available stored energy, recent charging and discharging activity, equipment availability, operating constraints, outage and derate history, and any competing market or reliability obligations. It should also account for usable energy capacity, temperature, degradation, conversion losses, and the feasibility of recharging before subsequent stress events. Where resource accreditation is at issue, the relevant hours, event weights, and assurance standard should be defined by the applicable resource-adequacy or accreditation methodology.
These distinctions become increasingly important as battery resources move from supplemental or opportunistic market participation toward material reliance in resource adequacy, ancillary services, and real-time operations. In that context, reliability accreditation should reflect installed MW, rated duration, and also the resource’s demonstrated and expected ability to provide sustained, dispatchable output during the hours when the system is most likely to need it.

What determines whether a BESS can provide the required grid-support response, sustain it for the required duration, and recover its capability afterward?

Several different capabilities must be distinguished. The inverter and its controls determine whether the BESS can provide the required response characteristics, such as frequency or voltage response. The resource’s operating condition—including its available energy (MWh) and SOC (an estimate of charge level referenced to defined limits, which may be reported as a percentage or, in ERCOT market systems, in MWh)—helps determine whether that response can be sustained and how the resource can recover afterward. Recovery also depends on charging capability, grid conditions, charging opportunities, and other service obligations.
Accordingly, advanced inverter capability and energy availability are complementary reliability issues. A BESS may possess the technical capability to respond rapidly, but system operators also need sufficient visibility into whether the resource can sustain the required response under the operating conditions that prevail when the service is needed.
ERCOT’s adopted requirement illustrates the distinction. Nodal Operating Guide Revision Request (NOGRR) 272, approved by the Public Utility Commission of Texas in November 2025, requires an inverter-based Energy Storage Resource (ESR) connected to the ERCOT Transmission Grid under an original Standard Generation Interconnection Agreement (SGIA) executed on or after April 1, 2026 to provide specified advanced grid support when within the inverter current limit. It requires model demonstration of the capability to maintain an internal voltage phasor in the sub-transient-to-transient timeframe and control that phasor to maintain synchronism with the grid. The requirement also applies to portions of modifications to otherwise exempt ESRs that add aggregate nameplate MW capacity on or after April 1, 2026. During the stakeholder process ERCOT stated that an ESR is not required to reserve its capacity or SOC to provide advanced grid support, and committed to work with stakeholders to develop a market-based framework to compensate ESRs if withholding headroom and maintaining SOC becomes necessary. NOGRR 272 therefore establishes a capability requirement for covered ESRs and modifications. It does not ensure that the energy and headroom needed to provide it will be available when a disturbance occurs.


What role does SOC play in determining a BESS’s available and sustained operating capability?

SOC is a fundamental input to determining how much energy a BESS has available and therefore how long a given MW output can be sustained. Installed MW alone does not establish sustained capability because a battery with the same nameplate rating can have materially different operating capability depending on its energy state and recent operating history.
SOC therefore should be treated as a reliability-relevant operating variable, not simply as an internal battery-management metric. At the same time, SOC should not be treated as the sole determinant of capability. Available MW, operating limits, duration, and other conditions also matter.
Power headroom and energy margins are needed for bidirectional active-power response. A BESS at or near full charge has limited energy margin to absorb additional energy in response to an over-frequency event, and a BESS near its minimum SOC has limited energy available to inject in response to an under-frequency event. Sustained symmetric active-power response may therefore require a narrower SOC operating range than energy arbitrage alone, depending on the response magnitude, duration, and resource limits.
SOC is already used in some market processes. Order No. 841 required Commission-jurisdictional RTOs and ISOs to account for SOC and related physical and operational characteristics of electric storage resources in their participation models, while allowing resources to self-manage SOC. In June 2024, ERCOT began requiring QSEs representing ESRs to submit planned, minimum, and maximum SOC in their Current Operating Plans and accounting for the SOC needed to support each ESR’s ancillary-service responsibility (NPRR 1186). Since December 2025, in awarding energy and ancillary services, ERCOT's real-time co-optimization (RTC+B) has also used the SOC reported by each ESR’s Qualified Scheduling Entity via telemetry. These measures address market participation, reliability unit commitment, dispatch, and ancillary-service feasibility. They do not by themselves establish that all advanced grid-support functions have adequate energy and headroom when needed, or that SOC definitions and validation are consistent across regions. Resource-adequacy accreditation raises a separate question: whether the applicable methodology adequately represents chronological energy limits, charging opportunities, and performance during system-risk intervals. The answers that follow address these remaining questions.

What information is needed by system operators to determine BESS capability accurately and reliably in planning and real-time operations?

System operators need information that translates a BESS resource’s operating condition into usable system capability. At minimum, that includes its available power, usable stored energy—or SOC together with the energy-capacity and operating-limit information needed to determine usable energy—sustainable duration, and applicable operating limits. The relevant information may be current or forward-looking, depending on the decision horizon.
Resource planning requires estimates of the dependable capability that BESS can provide under future system conditions. Real-time operations require information about the capability available at a particular operating point and how long that capability can be sustained. The objective is therefore not simply additional raw telemetry, but operationally useful information about actual and expected BESS capability.

How should such information be measured, validated, expressed consistently, and communicated to system operators?

BESS capability should be determined from operating data that describe the resource’s power capability, usable stored energy, SOC, operating limits, and other constraints relevant to the service being evaluated. Where capability is projected rather than directly observed, the estimate should identify the applicable time horizon and the assumptions used to derive it.
The information should be validated against metered charging and discharging, observed resource performance, and other available operating data. Validation should identify stale, inconsistent, or implausible values and should provide an indication of data quality and, where appropriate, uncertainty in estimated capability. Reported SOC is itself an estimate produced by the battery-management system; its accuracy depends on the estimation method, sensor accuracy, operating conditions, and calibration.
Capability should be expressed using common definitions, units, and time conventions so that system operators can interpret and compare information across BESS resources. At a minimum, the information should distinguish available MW, usable MWh, sustainable duration, applicable operating constraints, and the time to which the information applies.
This information should be communicated electronically through the applicable owner, operator, or QSE reporting arrangements to the relevant grid operational and planning systems at a frequency appropriate to the decision being made. Real-time operations may require frequent updates, while planning applications may rely on validated historical data and forward-looking capability estimates.

How should BESS operating-capability information be incorporated into resource-adequacy, unit-commitment, dispatch, and ancillary-service models?

Capability information has limited reliability value unless the models used for planning and operations can incorporate it. Resource-adequacy models should use appropriate measures of dependable BESS capability, while unit-commitment, dispatch, and ancillary-service models should incorporate current and expected energy availability and operating constraints when determining what the resource can provide.
The objective is not necessarily to increase the capacity attributed to BESS. It is to improve the accuracy with which BESS capability is recognized and scheduled. Better information may reveal that some existing capability has been treated conservatively because of uncertainty; in other cases, it may confirm that less capability is available than nameplate values suggest.
Reserving SOC and headroom for grid support has an opportunity cost, because reserving energy or power headroom may limit energy sales or other service revenues. If system operators come to rely on that reserved capability, the question of how it is compensated follows, as ERCOT acknowledged in the NOGRR 272 proceeding. Accurate capability information is needed to define any separately procured service and evaluate appropriate compensation.

Are the reliability events and operational trends prompting ERCOT’s BESS requirements also present in other regions?
Yes, in varying degrees. In Order No. 901 the Commission directed NERC to develop Reliability Standards for inverter-based resources (IBRs) based on performance problems that NERC documented in both the Western and Texas Interconnections. NERC has also published a nonbinding white paper containing functional specifications for grid-forming BESS connected to the bulk power system. The severity of these issues varies with IBR penetration, system strength, and available inertia, so the Commission, NERC, and the ISOs/RTOs should determine where comparable reliability concerns exist and what performance requirements are warranted under regional system conditions.

Should requirements similar to ERCOT’s advanced grid-support requirements for BESS be applied nationwide?

Not in identical form. Any national action should follow from the reliability need being addressed. Different regions have different resource mixes, network characteristics, operating conditions, and reliability needs. ERCOT in particular is connected to neighboring systems only through asynchronous ties, so it does not directly share their synchronous inertia. Controlled power transfers over those ties may provide frequency support, subject to their capabilities and operating arrangements. This asynchronous connection is one relevant consideration alongside IBR penetration, system strength, and stability constraints.
The more appropriate national role is therefore to establish common principles where a common reliability need exists, and to allow region-specific performance parameters consistent with applicable national Reliability Standards, rather than prescribe a particular control design or impose an identical implementation everywhere.

Should FERC establish common reliability principles for BESS while allowing ISOs and RTOs to set performance-based requirements according to regional system conditions?
Yes. Within its statutory authority, the Commission should establish common reliability principles for BESS while allowing regional implementation. Those principles should focus on measurable performance, accurate and usable information about actual capability, and incorporation of that information into reliability planning and system operations.
The Commission has several means to do this. First, building on the Reliability Standards developed under Order No. 901, including the IBR data and modeling standards approved in February 2026,  the Commission can review whether those standards adequately address the data BESS owners and operators provide to Reliability Coordinators, Balancing Authorities, and Transmission Operators, including available energy, SOC, and operating limits, and the representation of energy limits in planning and operational models. Where supported by the record, the Commission can direct NERC to develop new or modified standards under section 215(d)(5), subject to the limits of section 215. Second, the Commission can ask Commission-jurisdictional RTOs and ISOs to report how SOC and energy limits are reflected in resource-adequacy accreditation and ancillary-service qualification. FERC-approved Reliability Standards under section 215 of the Federal Power Act apply to covered entities and facilities within ERCOT according to each standard’s applicability and implementation plan; FERC’s pro forma interconnection requirements generally do not govern ERCOT interconnections. Section 215 does not authorize the Commission to order construction of additional generation or transmission capacity or to set and enforce adequacy standards. Resource-adequacy accreditation proposals must therefore distinguish reliability assessments from obligations imposed through jurisdictional market tariffs or state programs.
